In March 2024, Resmetirom (Rezdiffra) received FDA approval for treating adults with non-cirrhotic MASH and moderate to advanced liver fibrosis (Keam 20.

However, additional therapies targeting different mechanisms are still necessary to address the complexity of liver fibrosis and improve patient outcomes. 11β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β-HSD is an enzyme highly expressed in the liver and adipose tissue, responsible for converting inactive cortisone to active cortisol in humans (Joharapurkar et al. 2012; Gathercole et al. 2013; Rahimi et al. Active cortisol is a key glucocorticoid that regulates metabolism inflammation, and immune responses. 11β-HSD1 plays a crucial role in regulating hepatic glucose output and is implicated in intrahepatic fat deposition.

Elevated expression of 11β-HSD1 in visceral adipose tissue can promote adipogenesis, potentially leading to conditions such as Cushing’s disease (Bujalska et al. 1997; Gathercole et al. In addition, elevated A novel 11β‑HSD1 inhibitor ameliorates liver fibrosis by inhibiting the notch 11β-HSD1 activity has been implicated in the pathogenesis of MASH due to its role in promoting hepatic gluconeogenesis, lipogenesis, and insulin resistance.

Excess cortisol production in the liver exacerbates fat accumulation, contributing to hepatic steatosis and inflammation (Koh et al. 2015; Li et al. In the context of MASH, increased 11β-HSD1 activity enhances hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation and extracellular matrix deposition, leading to liver fibrosis.
Several selective 11β-HSD1 inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments for MASLD.

For example, the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor RO5093151 was tested in patients with insulin-resistant MASLD, leading to significant reductions in liver fat content and liver enzyme levels (Stefan et al. However, the study also reported notable adverse effects, including nervous system issues, gastrointestinal disturbances, and infections (Stefan et al. Another selective 11β-HSD1 inhibitor, AZD6925, demonstrated efficacy in reducing hepatic triglyceride accumulation, preventing liver steatosis, and enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis in db/db mice(Koh et al. Additionally, BVT.2733 has been shown to inhibit hepatic lipogenesis and lipolysis in fatty tissues of mice on a high-fat diet.

This led to reduced levels of glucocorticoids and free fatty acids delivered to the liver, thereby alleviating hepatic steatosis (Li et al. 2021; Ko et al. Collectively, these findings indicate that 11β- HSD1 plays a pivotal role in the progression of MASLD.
Recent research has highlighted J2H-1702 as a promising new 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for treating metabolic disorders and liver fibrosis.

Developed by another research group, J2H-1702 (2-((R)-4-(2-Fluoro-4-(methylsulfonyl) phenyl)-2-methylpiperazin-1-yl)-N-((1R,2S,3S,5S,7S)- 5-hydroxyadamantan-2-yl) pyrimidine-4-carboxamide) has shown significant efficacy in suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis, improving lipid profiles, and enhancing metabolic parameters (Oh et al. 2015; Ryu et al. This compound also reduced hepatic lipid accumulation and mitigated liver fibrosis by deactivating HSCs (Lee et al. In Phase 1 clinical trial, J2H-1702 was well-tolerated, with only mild adverse events reported.

Its pharmacokinetic profile exhibited dose-dependent exposure suitable for once-daily dosing within the therapeutic range (Kim et al. Currently, J2H-1702 is undergoing Phase 2 clinical trials to further evaluate its efficacy and safety in patients with MASLD.
Despite these findings, comprehensive research on the anti-fibrotic role of 11β-HSD1 inhibitor and its mechanism of action is still not sufficient.

Given the complex pathophysiology of liver fibrosis, effective therapeutic strategies should address not only hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation but also the immune mechanisms involved in fibrosis resolution.

Therefore, the aim of this study is to investigate the anti-fibrotic effect and to identify and characterize changes signaling pathway… 167 in immune cell populations for elucidating the mechanism of action of a novel 11β-HSD1 inhibitor and their potential as therapeutic agents for liver fibrosis.

Materials and methods Animal experiments and ethics statement C57BL/6J wild-type male mice (six weeks old) were obtained from Dae Han Bio Link (Eumseong, Republic of Korea) and maintained at the Hanyang Laboratory Animal Research Center.

The mice were randomly divided into four groups (Fig. 1A; n = 10 per group, total n = 4: a normal control group, a group receiving 0.03% thioacetamide (TAA; Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA; Cas. 62-55- 5) in drinking water for 19 weeks, a group treated with TAA + obeticholic acid (OCA, 10 mg/kg/day) as a positive control (APExBIO, Boston, MA, USA) for 9 weeks, and a group treated with TAA + 10 mg/kg/day 11β-HSD1 inhibitor (J2H Biotech, Suwon, Republic of Korea) for 9 weeks (Wallace et al. 2015; Liu et al. After 10 weeks of TAA exposure, the treatment groups received either OCA or the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor combined with TAA for an additional 9 weeks.

Both OCA and the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor were administered orally via gavage once daily (Neuschwander- Tetri et al. 2015; Goto et al. 2018; Younossi et al. This study was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Hanyang University (Approval No: HY-IACUC-21-00.
All experimental procedures were designed and conducted in compliance with the ethical guidelines established by the committee.

The following reagents were obtained for the study: OCA (APExBIO, Boston, MA, USA), TAA (163678-25G, Sigma-Aldrich, Missouri, USA), and Tgf-beta (240-B, R&D systems, Minnesota, USA).

Hydroxyproline assay The hydroxyproline assay was performed using the PicoSens™ Hydroxyproline Assay Kit (BM-HYP-100, Biomax) to quantify collagen content in liver tissues.

Frozen liver tissue samples (10 mg, n = 3 per group) were homogenized in 100 µL of concentrated HCl (12N) and hydrolyzed at 120 °C for 3 h. After hydrolysis, 10 µL of each sample was transferred to a 96-well microplate and evaporated completely using a 70 °C heat block.
A 0.1 mg/ mL Hydroxyproline Standard solution was prepared by diluting 10 µL of 1 mg/mL Hydroxyproline Standard with 90 µL of distilled water.

Standard curves were generated by dispensing 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 µL of the standard solution into wells, corresponding to 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1 µg/well, and evaporating the solutions at 70 °C. To initiate the reaction, 100 µL of Chloramine T Reagent was added to each well containing samples and standards, followed by incubation at room temperature for 5 min. Next, 100 µL of DMAB Reagent was added to each well, and the plate was incubated at 60 °C for 90 min. Absorbance was measured at 560 nm using a microplate reader.
The hydroxyproline content was calculated and expressed as µg/g of liver tissue.

Measurement of intracellular cortisol level LX-2 cells were seeded at a total density of 2 × 105 cells/ well in a 6 well cell culture dish (Falcon) at 37 °C for 24 h. LX-2 cells were treated with 10 μM cortisol and 1 μM 11β- HSD1 inhibitor at 37 °C for 24 h. After that, the conditioned medium of LX-2 cells was centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 3 min and the supernatant was collected.

Cortisol levels in conditioned medium and mouse liver tissue (n = 3 for each group) were measured using a Cortisol ELISA kit (ADI-900-071, enzolifescience) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and the absorbance was measured at a wavelength of 405 nm using an iMark Microplate Reader (Bio-rad).

RNA extraction and quantitative real‑time polymerase chain reaction (qRT‑PCR) Total RNA was extracted from liver tissue, LX-2 cells, and HepG2 cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen Co., Carlsbad, CA, USA; Cas No. 155960 (n = 8 per group).
Briefly, 1 mL of TRIzol and 0.2 mL of chloroform were added to liver tissue.
The mixture was centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatant was carefully collected.

To precipitate the RNA, 0.5 mL of isopropanol signaling pathway… 169 was added per 1 mL of TRIzol, followed by incubation at 4 °C for 10 min. The samples were then centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, and the RNA pellet was obtained.
RNA concentration and purity were assessed using a Nanodrop ND-2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Wilmington, DE, USA).
High-purity RNA with an A260/A280 absorbance ratio between 1.8 and 2.0 was considered suitable for further analysis.

For reverse transcription, 2 μg of total RNA was converted into complementary DNA (cDNA) using the PrimeScript™ RT Reagent Kit (Takara Bio, Kusatsu City, Shiga Prefecture, Japan; Cas No. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was conducted on a LightCycler 480 system (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany) with LightCycler 480 SYBR Green I Master Mix. Reactions were performed in triplicate in 96-well plates.
Expression levels were normalized to GAPDH and β-actin, which served as reference genes.
The primer sequences used are detailed in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2.

RNA sequencing analysis RNA sequencing was carried out by the Biospecimen- Multiomics Digital Bioanalysis Core Facility at Hanyang University on liver tissues from the following mouse groups (n = 3 per group): normal control, TAA-treated group, TAA + OCA group, TAA + 11β-HSD1 inhibitor responder group, and TAA + 11β-HSD1 inhibitor non-responder group.
In the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor group, mice were classified as responders if they exhibited fibrosis alleviation (fibrosis score ≤ 4) and reduced expression of fibrosis-related markers.
Mice that did not meet these criteria were classified as non-responders.
Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, USA).

RNA quality was assessed with an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Amstelveen, The Netherlands), and RNA concentration was measured with a Nanodrop ND-2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Wilmington, DE, USA).
The RNA concentration was further validated using Quant-IT RiboGreen (Invitrogen).
To determine the DV200 value (percentage of RNA fragments > 200 bp), samples were analyzed with TapeStation RNA ScreenTape (Agilent).
For library preparation, 100 ng of total RNA was processed using the Agilent SureSelect RNA Direct Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Briefly, the RNA was fragmented into smaller pieces by exposing it to divalent cations at elevated temperatures.
The fragmented RNA was reverse-transcribed into first-strand cDNA using random primers, followed by synthesis of the second strand.
The cDNA fragments were then subjected to end repair, A-tailing, and adapter ligation.
The resulting products were 1 70 purified and amplified via PCR to generate the final cDNA libraries.
The Mus musculus reference genome (mm and associated annotation data were obtained from the UCSC Table Browser (http://g enome.u csc.e du).
The aligned reads were assembled into transcripts and quantified using StringTie v2.1.3b, which provided relative abundance estimates as read counts for transcripts and genes.
The analysis included known transcripts, novel transcripts, and alternative splicing variants.
Expression levels were expressed as read counts or FPKM (Fragments Per Kilobase of exon per Million mapped fragments).
Further analysis to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was conducted using these expression profiles.

Adapters and low-quality reads (with scores below Q were removed using FASTX_ Trimmer (Lab 20 and BBMap (Bushnell 20.

The cleaned reads were then aligned to the reference genome using TopHat (Trapnell et al. Gene expression levels were estimated from the FPKM values generated by Cufflinks (Roberts et al. These expression values were normalized using the quantile normalization method implemented in EdgeR within the R statistical environment.
To visualize differential expression results, a volcano plot was generated.
The X-axis represents the log2 fold change, while the Y-axis represents the − log10 p-value derived from comparing the group averages.

Immune profiling of mouse peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) by mass cytometry The immunological mechanism of action of the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor was investigated by analyzing changes in immune cell populations in mouse PMBC samples using mass cytometry.
The study included three groups: normal control (n = 5), TAA-treated (n = 6), and TAA + 11β-HSD1 inhibitor-treated (n = 8) groups.

Detailed procedures are described in previous research (Bae et al. Data processing and visualization were conducted using Cytobank (https://w ww.c ytoba nk.o rg).

Immune cell types and subtypes were identified using a manual gating strategy (Supplementary Table S4 and Fig. To visualize data at single-cell resolution, the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) algorithm was applied for dimensionality reduction.

Additionally, automated clustering methods such as PhenoGraph and Citrus were utilized to complement manual gating (Supplementary Table S. Samples containing fewer than 1000 cells were excluded from the final analysis.
In the mass cytometry data, approximately 20% of cells remained unclassified, while the remaining cells were identified as leukocytes.

Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using the GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Software, Inc., San Diego, CA, USA).
All data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD).
The Mann–Whitney U test was used to analyze data that did not follow a normal distribution, as determined by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test.
For comparisons involving multiple groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was applied.
When significant differences were detected, Tukey’s post-hoc test was used for pairwise comparisons, assuming homogeneity of variances.
A p-value of less than 0.05 (p < 0. was considered to indicate statistical significance.

Results 11β‑HSD1 inhibition reduces liver fibrosis, inflammation, and intracellular cortisol levels in animal and in vitro models 11β-HSD1 inhibitor treatment decreased hepatocyte ballooning (H&E staining, Fig. 1B, C, and Table S, fibrosis area (Sirius Red staining, p = 0.0015; Fig. 1B, D, and Table S, and ALT and AST levels (Fig. 1E and Table S compared to the TAA-induced liver fibrosis model.

Sirius Red staining showed that collagen deposition was significantly increased in the TAA group compared to the NC group (Fig. Treatment with both OCA and the 11β- HSD1 inhibitor reduced collagen deposition, with the 11β- HSD1 inhibitor showing a similar reduction (Fig. The normal control group showed steady weight gain and lower liver weights, while the TAA-treated group exhibited significantly lower body weights and increased liver weights, with both the TAA + OCA and TAA + 11β-HSD1 inhibitor groups partially mitigating the TAA-induced changes (Fig. 1F, G and Supplementary Tables S9, S. RT-PCR in the liver tissues showed that 11β-HSD1 inhibition significantly decreased fibrosis markers (α-Sma, Col1a1, Fn1, and Timp and inflammation markers (Il-6, Mcp1, Nlrp3, and Tnf-α) compared to the TAA-treated group (Fig. In vitro, LX-2 and HepG2 cells treated with 1 μM 11β-HSD1 inhibitor, after fibrosis and inflammation induction by TGF-β (20 ng/mL) and TAA (0.02 g/ mL), respectively, exhibited significantly decreased expression of fibrosis markers (α-SMA, COL1A1, and TIMP and inflammation markers (IL6, MCP1 and signaling pathway… 171 NLRP compared to untreated induced groups (Fig. Additionally, protein expression levels of fibrosis markers (Col1a1, Fn-1 and Vimentin) and inflammation markers (Il-6 and Nlrp were decreased in the liver tissues of the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor group compared to the TAA-treated group (Fig. To further quantify collagen deposition and validate the anti-fibrotic effects of the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor, we measured the hydroxyproline content in liver tissues (Fig. 2D), hydroxyproline levels were significantly increased in the TAA-treated group compared to the NC group.
Treatment with the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor significantly reduced hydroxyproline levels compared to the TAA group, indicating a marked reduction in collagen accumulation.

To clarify whether the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor directly targets 11β-HSD1 or acts through competitive inhibition, we measured the mRNA levels of 11β-HSD1 in mouse liver tissues and LX-2 cells (Fig. 11β-HSD1 mRNA expression was significantly elevated in the TAA-treated group compared to the NC. Treatment with the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor significantly reduced 11β-HSD1 mRNA levels in TAA-induced fibrotic mouse liver tissues.
Similarly, in LX-2 cells treated with cortisol (10 μM), 11β-HSD1 mRNA expression was significantly upregulated compared to the normal control.
Co-treatment with the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor (1 μM) led to a significant reduction in 11β- HSD1 mRNA levels.

These results suggest that J2H-1702 directly suppresses 11β-HSD1 expression, further supporting the mechanism of action by which the inhibitor reduces intracellular cortisol levels and alleviates fibrosis.

To investigate whether the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor exerts its effects via modulation of intracellular cortisol levels, we measured the expression of fibrosis markers in LX-2 cells treated with cortisol (10 μM) in the presence or absence of inhibitor (1 μM).

Cortisol treatment significantly increased the mRNA levels of Col1a1 and Fn1 compared to the normal control (Fig. Co-treatment with 11β-HSD1 inhibitor significantly reduced the expression of both Col1a1 and Fn1, suggesting that J2H-1702 directly suppresses HSC activation through the reduction of intracellular cortisol levels.
These results provide further evidence that the anti-fibrotic effects of 11β-HSD1 inhibitor are mediated through intracellular glucocorticoid modulation.
In addition, we measured intracellular cortisol levels in both LX-2 cells and mouse liver tissues (Fig. Cortisol levels were significantly elevated in the TAA-treated group compared to the NC group.
Treatment with 11β-HSD1 inhibitor significantly reduced intracellular cortisol levels in liver tissues of the TAA group.
Similarly, in LX-2 cells treated with cortisol, intracellular cortisol levels were significantly reduced when co-treated with 11β-HSD1 inhibitor.

Consequently, the reduction in the B cell population observed after 11β-HSD1 inhibitor treatment could be associated with the amelioration of liver fibrosis and inflammation (Patel et al. 2021; Bae et al. Recent studies have highlighted the therapeutic potential of NK cells in alleviating liver fibrosis (Yang et al. 2021; Xu et al. For example, studies in a CCl₄-induced liver cirrhosis mouse model have shown that activated NK cells can substantially reduce cirrhosis by decreasing collagen deposition, HSC activation, and macrophage infiltration (Oh et al. These findings suggest that NK cell presence and activity are crucial for reducing liver fibrosis and inflammation through their ability to target activated HSCs and modulate immune responses.

OCA is a farnesoid X receptor (FXR) agonist that has shown efficacy in preclinical and clinical studies for reducing liver fibrosis and inflammation in models of MASH and NASH (Neuschwander-Tetri et al. Due to its dual role in improving hepatic lipid metabolism and reducing fibrosis progression, OCA is widely recognized as a benchmark for evaluating new therapeutic candidates in liver fibrosis models.

In addition, OCA was granted accelerated approval by the U.S. FDA for the treatment of primary biliary cholangitis and has been evaluated in Phase 3 clinical trials for MASH with fibrosis (Younossi et al. Its established use in clinical settings for liver diseases makes it a clinically relevant comparator for evaluating the efficacy of novel anti-fibrotic agents like the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor.
To investigate the gene expression changes induced by TAA and 11β-HSD1 inhibition, RNA sequencing was conducted on liver tissue.
This analysis aimed to uncover potential mechanisms through which 11β-HSD1 inhibition alleviates liver fibrosis.

RNA sequencing and KEGG pathway analysis identified several significantly enriched pathways, with the Notch signaling pathway ranking highest (Supplementary Table S: Notch signaling pathway was the most significantly downregulated among several pathways following 11β-HSD1 inhibition.

Given its established role in hepatic stellate cell activation and liver fibrosis, the Notch pathway was selected for further investigation (Bansal et al. The ERBB and JAK-STAT pathways were also evaluated due to their involvement in cell proliferation and immune regulation, respectively.
Activation of the Notch signaling pathway is known to drive the transformation of HSCs into myofibroblasts, contributing to liver fibrosis progression (Adams and Jafar- Nejad 20.
Specifically, when Notch signaling is activated in hepatocytes, the secretion of Spp1 (Opn) is enhanced, which stimulates myofibroblast differentiation (Adams and Jafar-Nejad 20.

In contrast, inhibition of Notch signaling signaling pathway… 177 triggers liver sinusoidal endothelial cells to produce nitric oxide, which suppresses the differentiation of HSCs into myofibroblasts.
Furthermore, disruption of Notch signaling in myofibroblasts has been shown to attenuate liver fibrosis by modulating both the progression and regression of fibrosis (Yue et al. 2021; Xu and Wang 20.

Yue et al. (20 demonstrated that blocking Notch signaling specifically in myofibroblasts reduced HSC activation during fibrosis progression and promoted extracellular matrix degradation and myofibroblast apoptosis during fibrosis regression.

This dual function highlights the significance of Notch signaling in both advancing and resolving liver fibrosis, suggesting that the anti-fibrotic effects of 11β-HSD1 inhibitors may be mediated through the modulation of this pathway.
Our findings demonstrate that inhibition of 11β-HSD1 suppresses the activation of HSCs and liver fibrosis via modulation of the Notch signaling pathway.
This aligns with previous research showing the critical role of Notch1 signaling in HSC activation and fibrogenesis.

Specifically, a study by Yang et al. demonstrated that Notch1 activation in HSCs contributes significantly to liver fibrosis, as mice lacking Notch1 in HSCs exhibited reduced fibrogenic responses (Yang et al. The study further identified that Notch1 is upregulated in response to hyaluronan production, promoting fibrogenic and proliferative phenotypes of HSCs.

This mechanistic insight highlights the importance of Notch1 in maintaining the fibrotic phenotype and supports our observation that 11β-HSD1 inhibition reduces Notch signaling, thereby ameliorating liver fibrosis.
Targeting this pathway could be a promising strategy for treating liver fibrosis, particularly in conditions such as MASH.
GO analysis of the liver transcriptomic data revealed significant changes in the expression of genes related to fibrosis and NK cell activation.
In the TAA-induced liver fibrosis model, the expression levels of NK cell activationrelated genes, such as Il15ra, Il18, Lyst, and Tox, were notably affected.

In contrast, treatment with the 11β-HSD1 inhibitor led to opposing changes in these gene expressions (Supplementary Table S. These findings indicate that 11β-HSD1 inhibition may influence NK cell-mediated immune responses.
Furthermore, results from mass cytometry analysis showed a reduction in the NK cell population in the TAA-induced liver fibrosis model compared to normal controls.
This reduction was significantly reversed following 11β-HSD1 inhibitor treatment.
NK cells are known to contribute to anti-fibrotic processes in the liver by inhibiting HSCs either directly or through the secretion of cytokines.
However, additional research is necessary to substantiate these observations.
Meanwhile, Conflicting results regarding the role of 11β- HSD1 inhibition in liver fibrosis have also been reported.

For example, Xiao et al. (20 found a positive correlation between 11β-HSD1 expression and typical markers of 1 78 liver fibrosis, demonstrating that inhibition of 11β-HSD1 with BVT.2733 significantly reduced fibrosis (Xiao et al. In contrast, another study reported that inhibition of 11β-HSD1 by UE2316 activated hepatic myofibroblasts and exacerbated liver fibrosis in a mouse model of reversible carbon tetrachloride-induced liver fibrosis (Zou et al. This research suggested that the function of 11β-HSD1 during liver injury and repair is context-dependent, emphasizing the importance of the timing of inhibitor administration (Zou et al. The discrepancies in these findings may arise from differences in liver injury models and the specific timing of 11β-HSD1 inhibitor treatment.

Our study, supported by comprehensive immune cell profiling via mass cytometry, highlights that 11β-HSD1 inhibition with J2H-1702 not only exerts direct effects on hepatic myofibroblasts but also significantly enhances the liver immune environment by modulating NK cell populations.
These findings suggest that the therapeutic benefits of J2H-1702 extend beyond its impact on myofibroblasts to include broader improvements in immune function within the liver.
Our findings are consistent with those of Xiao et al. (20, who demonstrated that 11β-HSD1 plays a crucial role in the activation of HSCs and the progression of liver fibrosis.

Results from our RNA sequencing and subsequent analyses revealed that 11β-HSD1 inhibition significantly suppressed the Notch signaling pathway, supporting its role in driving the differentiation and activation of HSCs into myofibroblasts.

Additionally, the observed increase in NK cell populations following 11β-HSD1 inhibition corresponds with a reduction in fibrosis markers, suggesting a potential mechanism through which NK cells mediate anti-fibrotic effects.
These results support the idea that 11β-HSD1 inhibition not only directly influences HSC activity but also modulates the immune microenvironment to enhance anti-fibrotic responses.
In conclusion, inhibiting 11β-HSD1 demonstrates promise in mitigating liver fibrosis in a mouse model.
This therapeutic effect appears to be associated with the suppression of the Notch signaling pathway.
Furthermore, the increase in NK cell populations following 11β-HSD1 inhibition highlights the role of NK cell-mediated immune responses in the observed anti-fibrotic effects.
Given that MASH is characterized by metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and progressive fibrosis, 11β-HSD1 inhibitors like J2H-1702 offer a multifaceted therapeutic approach.

By simultaneously reducing cortisol-induced metabolic dysregulation, inhibiting pro-fibrotic signaling pathways, and enhancing immune-mediated clearance of HSCs, 11β-HSD1 inhibition holds promise as an effective treatment for MASH.
